mappings.note: Peels the lower leaf surface, stains it and looks for pores under the microscope: an observation made through a prepared investigation.
Two tumblers, one with red water, compared the next day and the cut stem examined: a controlled experiment with recorded observations.
The boil, decolourise and iodine procedure for testing a leaf for starch: the investigation itself.
Traces potato starch back to glucose made in the leaves and moved down the plant: the process explained across organs. Not LO-132, since no test is being run.
Broad flat leaves are efficient because the larger area catches more light and holds more stomata: form tied to its consequence.
Fills in glucose, oxygen and water in the respiration word equation, which LO-135 names explicitly.

Which leaves will pass the iodine test, with the printed answer discussing the sunlight-deprived plant: either way the item is about what the starch test shows under different conditions. The stray answer text is reported as a defect.
Hydrilla in sunlight against the same in the dark, with the collected gas tested by a glowing splint: an experiment and its inference.
Asks the student to design the warm-against-cold water transport experiment: investigation planning, which LO-132 covers.
Photosynthesis and respiration each supplying what the other needs: two processes explained as a cycle. Not LO-142, because no protective action is asked of the student.
Plants making their own food from simple substances rather than eating: the defining process stated.
New leaves, greater height and a thickening stem as the visible signs of growth: features identified by observation.
Reads the watered and unwatered pots against each other to conclude that water is essential: an inference from the controlled comparison.
The same experiment read for the light variable, comparing the lit pot with the one in the dark.
Compares lime water in two tubes, one fed from the flask of germinating seeds: the observation and its meaning within the set-up.
Imagines the loss of all photosynthesising organisms and follows the consequences for food and oxygen: the importance of the process argued out. Not LO-142, since no conservation action is involved.
Ranks the pots by growth from the recorded observations of the three-pot experiment.
Works out in which set-ups starch forms and oxygen is released by checking which requirement each one lacks: reading a multi-condition experiment.
Identifies what Ananya's four tubes with snail, plant and carbon dioxide indicator are meant to find out and how she would know: reading an investigation's purpose and evidence.
A variegated leaf from a plant kept in the dark shows no colour anywhere, and the inference has to be drawn from the table of results.
Fills the results table for the leaf partly enclosed in a bottle and states what the experiment shows.
Vrikshayurveda as an ancient text on plant care and soil: a piece of scientific heritage to appreciate.
Starch as the storage form of the food plants make: an output of the process.
The leaf as the main site of photosynthesis: where in the plant the process runs. Not LO-129, because the leaf is not being identified from its features.
Names chlorophyll, the green pigment of leaves: identification of a component by the colour it gives.
Why the leaf is boiled in alcohol, namely to strip the chlorophyll so the iodine colour shows: a step of the procedure justified.
Blue-black with iodine as the reading for starch: how the test's result is interpreted.
Starch appearing only in the green patches ties starch production to the presence of chlorophyll: result related to cause. Not LO-132, because the result is given and the conclusion is what is asked.
No starch even in green patches after darkness ties production to light: the same reasoning for the other requirement.
Red or brown leaves explained by other pigments masking chlorophyll: appearance traced to its cause rather than merely noted.
Caustic soda is there to soak up the carbon dioxide inside the bottle: the purpose of a control in the set-up.
Only the part outside the bottle makes starch, so carbon dioxide is shown to be necessary: the conclusion of that same experiment.
Names photosynthesis as the whole food-making process.
Oxygen as the by-product alongside glucose: a product of the photosynthesis relation that LO-135 names.
Picks the correct word equation for photosynthesis, with its inputs, conditions and outputs.
R.H. Dastur and his work on the factors affecting photosynthesis: a scientist's story.
Names the stomata, the pores on the leaf surface: identification of a structure.
Roots taking up water and dissolved minerals: the uptake step of the plant's transport process.
Names the xylem as the tubes carrying water upward: identification of a tissue.
The red dye reaching stem, leaves and flowers is read as evidence of xylem transport: a conclusion from the experiment rather than a definition.
